meta.rendering_note: All math is written as single, unnested KaTeX spans: the magnetic moment appears as \( \vec m \) or \( m \), the permeability constant as \( \mu_0 \), and Greek-letter symbols such as \( \chi \), \( \theta \) and \( \delta \) always sit inside KaTeX, never as raw Unicode. No raw Unicode math symbols, arrows included, appear anywhere. Diamagnetic susceptibility is always reported negative, and every numeric answer terminates cleanly or is a clean order-of-magnitude value.

topics.name: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
topics.summary: A bar magnet behaves as a magnetic dipole with moment \( \vec m \), pointing from its S pole to its N pole and measured in \( \text{A m}^2 \). Its field lines leave the N pole, curve around outside, enter the S pole, and then continue inside the magnet from S back to N, so every line is a closed loop. This is the key difference from electric field lines, which begin and end on charges. Far from a short magnet, the field mirrors an electric dipole's with \( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \) replaced by \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \): on the axis it is \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3} \), along \( \vec m \), and on the equatorial line it is \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^3} \), opposite to \( \vec m \). At equal distances the axial field is exactly twice the equatorial one, and both fall as \( 1/r^3 \). Because field lines form closed loops, the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero. This is Gauss's law for magnetism, and it tells us that isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist: cutting a magnet only makes smaller complete magnets.
topics.worked_example:
A short magnet has \( m=0.5\ \text{A m}^2 \). Find the fields at 0.1 m on its axis and on its equatorial line.

Axial: \( 10^{-7}\times\dfrac{2\times0.5}{(0.1)^3}=10^{-4} \) T, along \( \vec m \).

Equatorial: \( 10^{-7}\times\dfrac{0.5}{(0.1)^3}=5\times10^{-5} \) T, opposite to \( \vec m \). The ratio is \( 2:1 \).
common_mistakes: Swapping the axial and equatorial formulas, or reversing their 2:1 ratio.
Using \( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \) instead of \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \) in a magnetic field formula.
Using \( 1/r^2 \) instead of \( 1/r^3 \) for a dipole field.
Thinking field lines stop at the N pole instead of continuing from S to N inside the magnet.
Believing a magnet can be cut to isolate a single N or S pole.

topics.name: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
topics.summary: A bar magnet in a uniform field feels no net force, because the forces on its two poles cancel, but it does feel a torque \( \vec\tau=\vec m\times\vec B \), of magnitude \( mB\sin\theta \), where \( \theta \) is the angle between \( \vec m \) and \( \vec B \). The torque is zero at \( 0^\circ \) and \( 180^\circ \) and greatest at \( 90^\circ \). The potential energy is \( U=-\vec m\cdot\vec B=-mB\cos\theta \). It is lowest, \( -mB \), when the magnet is aligned with the field: this is stable equilibrium. It is highest, \( +mB \), when the magnet is anti-aligned: this is unstable equilibrium, and a slight nudge sends the magnet swinging away. The work needed to turn a magnet from one angle to another equals the change in \( U \), so a full flip from aligned to anti-aligned costs \( 2mB \). Displaced slightly from the aligned position, the magnet oscillates in SHM with period \( T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mB}} \), where \( I \) is its moment of inertia. This holds only for small angles, where \( \sin\theta\approx\theta \). Gravity and length play no part, so the pendulum formula does not apply.
topics.worked_example:
A magnet with \( I=5\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^2 \) and \( m=0.5\ \text{A m}^2 \) oscillates with small amplitude in a 0.04 T field.

\( \dfrac{I}{mB}=\dfrac{5\times10^{-3}}{0.02}=0.25\ \text{s}^2 \).

\( T=2\pi\sqrt{0.25}=\pi \) s.
common_mistakes: Calling the anti-aligned (\( 180^\circ \)) position stable; it is the maximum-energy, unstable position.
Using \( \cos\theta \) for torque or \( \sin\theta \) for energy.
Writing the period as \( 2\pi\sqrt{L/g} \) or inverting \( \dfrac{I}{mB} \).
Forgetting the minus sign in \( U=-mB\cos\theta \) when finding work.
Applying the SHM period to large-amplitude swings.

topics.name: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
topics.summary: Earth's magnetic field at any place is described by three elements. Declination is the angle, in the horizontal plane, between the geographic meridian (true north) and the magnetic meridian (where a compass points). Dip, or inclination, is the angle the total field makes with the horizontal, measured in the magnetic meridian. It is \( 0^\circ \) at the magnetic equator, where the field is horizontal, and \( 90^\circ \) at the magnetic poles, where it is vertical. The third element is the horizontal component \( B_H \). With total field \( B \) and dip \( \delta \), the components are \( B_H=B\cos\delta \) and \( B_V=B\sin\delta \), so \( \tan\delta=\dfrac{B_V}{B_H} \) and \( B^2=B_H^2+B_V^2 \). A compass or a horizontally swinging magnet responds only to \( B_H \), which vanishes at the magnetic poles. Earth behaves roughly like a bar magnet whose S pole lies near geographic north, which is why a compass's N end points north. The field is believed to come from electric currents in the moving molten outer core (the dynamo effect), not from a permanent magnet, since the core is far above iron's Curie temperature.
topics.worked_example:
At a place, \( B=5\times10^{-5} \) T and the dip is \( 60^\circ \).

\( B_H=5\times10^{-5}\times\cos60^\circ=2.5\times10^{-5} \) T.

\( B_V=5\times10^{-5}\times\sin60^\circ=2.5\sqrt3\times10^{-5} \) T, and \( \dfrac{B_V}{B_H}=\sqrt3=\tan60^\circ \).
common_mistakes: Confusing declination (horizontal-plane angle from true north) with dip (angle below the horizontal).
Using \( \sin\delta \) for \( B_H \) or \( \cos\delta \) for \( B_V \).
Inverting \( \tan\delta=\dfrac{B_V}{B_H} \).
Adding \( B_H \) and \( B_V \) as scalars instead of by Pythagoras.
Thinking \( B_H \) is largest at the poles; it is zero there.

topics.name: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
topics.summary: When a material is placed in a magnetizing field, its atomic moments give it a net magnetic moment. Magnetization \( M \) is that net moment per unit volume, measured in A/m. Magnetic intensity \( H \) describes the magnetizing effect of free currents; inside a long solenoid \( H=nI \), also in A/m, whether or not a core is present. The actual field combines both: \( B=\mu_0(H+M) \), with \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A. Using \( B=\mu_0H \) alone treats the material as vacuum. Susceptibility \( \chi=\dfrac{M}{H} \) is dimensionless and measures how readily the material magnetizes. It is small and negative for diamagnets, small and positive for paramagnets, and very large for ferromagnets. Relative permeability is \( \mu_r=1+\chi \), and the permeability is \( \mu=\mu_0\mu_r \), so \( B=\mu H \). The quantities \( \chi \) and \( \mu_r \) always differ by exactly 1, and confusing them is a common source of error: a material with \( \mu_r=500 \) has \( \chi=499 \), and a diamagnet with \( \chi=-10^{-5} \) has \( \mu_r \) just below 1, never a negative permeability.
topics.worked_example:
A solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carries 2 A around a core of \( \mu_r=400 \).

\( H=nI=2000 \) A/m and \( \chi=399 \), so \( M=\chi H=7.98\times10^{5} \) A/m.

\( B=\mu_0\mu_rH=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times400\times2000=0.32\pi \) T.
common_mistakes: Using \( B=\mu_0H \) when a magnetized material is present.
Adding \( H \) and \( M \) without the factor \( \mu_0 \).
Treating \( \chi \) and \( \mu_r \) as the same, dropping the 1.
Reporting a positive \( \chi \) for a diamagnet.
Thinking a core changes \( H \); it changes \( M \) and \( B \).

topics.name: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
topics.summary: Materials fall into three classes. Diamagnetic substances, such as bismuth, copper and water, have small negative \( \chi \), are weakly repelled by a magnet, and show susceptibility that is essentially independent of temperature. A superconductor is a perfect diamagnet with \( \chi=-1 \), expelling the field completely. Paramagnetic substances, such as aluminium, sodium and oxygen, have small positive \( \chi \) and are weakly attracted. Their susceptibility obeys Curie's law, \( \chi=\dfrac{C}{T} \), so it falls as temperature rises; temperatures must be in kelvin. Ferromagnetic substances, namely iron, cobalt and nickel, have very large positive \( \chi \) because of aligned domains. Above the Curie temperature \( T_C \) this order breaks down and they become merely paramagnetic. A ferromagnet's B-H curve forms a hysteresis loop. Retentivity is the \( B \) left when \( H \) returns to zero; coercivity is the reverse \( H \) needed to bring \( B \) to zero. The loop area equals the energy lost per unit volume per cycle. Permanent magnets need high retentivity and high coercivity, a hard material. Electromagnet and transformer cores need low coercivity and a thin, low-loss loop, a soft material.
topics.worked_example:
A paramagnet has \( \chi=3\times10^{-4} \) at \( -73^\circ\text{C} \). Find \( \chi \) at \( 327^\circ\text{C} \).

In kelvin: 200 K and 600 K.

\( \chi_2=3\times10^{-4}\times\dfrac{200}{600}=10^{-4} \).
common_mistakes: Swapping 'attracted' and 'repelled' between paramagnets and diamagnets.
Letting paramagnetic \( \chi \) rise with temperature, or using Celsius in Curie's law.
Believing a ferromagnet stays ferromagnetic above \( T_C \).
Confusing retentivity (a \( B \) value) with coercivity (an \( H \) value).
Choosing a soft, low-coercivity material for a permanent magnet, or a hard one for an electromagnet core.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do the magnetic field lines run?
options: From the N pole to the S pole
From the S pole to the N pole
They leave the N pole and simply end at the S pole, with no lines inside the magnet
Straight and parallel to the magnet's axis everywhere
questions.explanation:
Outside the magnet, field lines emerge from the N pole, curve around, and enter the S pole.

Inside the magnet they continue from S back to N, so every line is a closed loop.
questions.hint: A compass needle's N end points along the field. Which way does it point near a magnet's N pole?
distractor_logic: Reverses the external direction; S-to-N is the direction of the lines only inside the magnet.
Treats magnetic lines like electric lines that terminate; magnetic field lines are closed loops that continue through the magnet.
Ignores the curved loop pattern; only a uniform field has straight parallel lines.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: Inside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines run
options: From the N pole to the S pole, the same as outside
From the S pole to the N pole, completing closed loops
Nowhere, because field lines stop at the poles
In random directions that cancel to zero
questions.explanation:
Magnetic field lines have no starting or ending points.

Having gone from N to S outside, each line returns from S to N inside the magnet to close the loop.
questions.hint: Closed loop: whatever goes out one way must come back the other way.
distractor_logic: Copies the outside direction; a closed loop must return from S to N inside the magnet.
Treats poles like charges that act as sources and sinks; magnetic lines never start or end.
Assumes a zero interior field; the inside of a magnet carries a strong field along \( \vec m \).

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: What is the net magnetic flux through any closed surface?
options: \( \mu_0 \) times the net pole strength enclosed
Positive whenever the surface encloses an N pole
\( \mu_0 \) times the current passing through the surface
questions.explanation:
Gauss's law for magnetism: \( \oint \vec B\cdot d\vec A=0 \).

Because every field line is a closed loop, each line that enters a closed surface also leaves it, so the net flux is zero.
questions.hint: Count how many times a closed loop crosses a closed surface going in, and how many times coming out.
distractor_logic: Copies Gauss's law for electricity (charge over \( \epsilon_0 \)); there is no free magnetic charge, so the flux is zero.
Assumes an N pole can be enclosed by itself; lines leaving a closed surface are always balanced by lines entering.
Mixes up Gauss's law with Ampere's circuital law, which concerns a closed loop, not a closed surface.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: Gauss's law for magnetism directly implies that
options: Cutting a bar magnet in the middle separates its N pole from its S pole
Magnetic field lines start on N poles and end on S poles
The magnetic field of a bar magnet is zero inside it
Isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist
questions.explanation:
Zero net flux through every closed surface means no net magnetic 'charge' can be enclosed anywhere.

So a single N or S pole can never exist on its own; poles always come in N-S pairs.
questions.hint: Electric flux can be non-zero because charges exist. What does zero magnetic flux say about magnetic 'charges'?
distractor_logic: Cutting only produces smaller complete magnets, each with its own N and S poles.
Treats magnetic lines like electric lines; zero net flux requires the lines to form closed loops.
The interior field is strong and runs from S to N; zero flux does not mean zero field.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: For a short bar magnet, the ratio of the field magnitude at a point on its axis to that at a point on its equatorial line, at the same distance, is
questions.explanation:
\( B_{axial}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3} \) and \( B_{equatorial}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^3} \).

At the same \( r \) their ratio is \( 2:1 \), exactly as for an electric dipole.
questions.hint: Recall the electric dipole: the axial field carries an extra factor of 2.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; the axial field is the larger of the two.
Assumes the field depends only on distance, ignoring the factor 2 in the axial formula.
Cubes the factor 2 as though it were a distance ratio inside the \( 1/r^3 \) law.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: The magnitude of the magnetic field at distance \( r \) on the axis of a short bar magnet of moment \( m \) is
questions.explanation:
A short bar magnet is a magnetic dipole. Its axial field mirrors the electric dipole's, with \( \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \) replaced by \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \) and \( p \) by \( m \).

So \( B_{axial}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3} \).
questions.hint: Axial means the factor 2; dipole means \( 1/r^3 \).
distractor_logic: This is the equatorial-line field; the axial field has the extra factor 2.
Uses the electric constant; the magnetic dipole formula uses \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \).
Uses an inverse-square law as for a single pole or point charge; a dipole field falls as \( 1/r^3 \).

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: Far from a short bar magnet, its field magnitude varies with distance \( r \) as
questions.explanation:
Both the axial and the equatorial fields of a dipole have \( r^3 \) in the denominator.

The fields of the two opposite poles nearly cancel far away, leaving a fall-off faster than inverse square: \( 1/r^3 \).
questions.hint: Same distance law as for an electric dipole.
distractor_logic: That is the fall-off for a single point charge or isolated pole, which does not exist magnetically.
That is the fall-off for the field of a long straight current-carrying wire.
Overcounts the cancellation between the poles; the dipole field goes as \( 1/r^3 \).

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: At a point on the equatorial line of a bar magnet, the direction of \( \vec B \) is
options: Perpendicular to the magnet, directed away from it
Zero, since the point is equidistant from both poles
questions.explanation:
On the equatorial line, the perpendicular components of the fields from the two poles cancel.

The components parallel to the axis add and point from the N-pole side toward the S-pole side, i.e. opposite to \( \vec m \), which points from S to N.
questions.hint: Trace a field line from the N pole around to the S pole. Which way does it point as it passes the middle?
distractor_logic: That is the direction on the axial line, not on the equatorial line.
Treats the magnet like a single pole radiating outward.
Only the components perpendicular to the axis cancel; the components parallel to the axis add.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: The torque on a magnetic dipole \( \vec m \) in a uniform field \( \vec B \) is
questions.explanation:
Torque is the cross product \( \vec m\times\vec B \), with magnitude \( mB\sin\theta \).

It tends to rotate \( \vec m \) into line with \( \vec B \).
questions.hint: Torque is a vector, and order matters in a cross product.
distractor_logic: Reverses the order of the cross product, flipping the direction of the torque.
Uses a dot product, which gives a scalar, not a turning vector.
This is the potential energy, not the torque.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: The potential energy of a magnetic dipole in a uniform field, with angle \( \theta \) between \( \vec m \) and \( \vec B \), is
questions.explanation:
\( U=-\vec m\cdot\vec B=-mB\cos\theta \).

The minus sign makes \( U \) lowest when \( \vec m \) is along \( \vec B \).
questions.hint: Energy is a dot product with a minus sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the minus sign, which would make the aligned position the least stable.
Uses sine; energy comes from the dot product, which uses cosine.
This is the torque magnitude, not the energy.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A bar magnet in a uniform field is in stable equilibrium when the angle between \( \vec m \) and \( \vec B \) is
questions.explanation:
At \( \theta=0^\circ \), the torque is zero and \( U=-mB \), its minimum value.

A small twist creates a torque that pushes the magnet back, so this equilibrium is stable.
questions.hint: Stable equilibrium sits at the lowest potential energy.
distractor_logic: Swaps stable and unstable; anti-alignment gives the maximum energy.
Torque is maximum there, so it is not an equilibrium at all.
No special property; the torque is non-zero at this angle.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: The torque on a bar magnet in a uniform field is greatest when \( \theta \) equals
questions.explanation:
\( \tau=mB\sin\theta \) is largest when \( \sin\theta=1 \), i.e. at \( \theta=90^\circ \).

At \( 0^\circ \) and \( 180^\circ \) the torque vanishes.
questions.hint: Where is \( \sin\theta \) largest?
distractor_logic: This is the stable position, where the torque is zero.
This is the unstable position, where the torque is also zero.
Picks an intermediate angle; \( \sin60^\circ \) is less than 1.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: The potential energy of a bar magnet in a uniform field is greatest when
questions.explanation:
\( U=-mB\cos\theta \) is largest when \( \cos\theta=-1 \), i.e. \( \theta=180^\circ \).

This anti-aligned position is an unstable equilibrium.
questions.hint: Make \( -\cos\theta \) as large as possible.
distractor_logic: Swaps the orientations; parallel alignment gives the lowest energy.
Confuses maximum torque with maximum energy; \( U=0 \) there.
Energy at this angle is negative, well below its maximum.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A bar magnet of moment \( m \) and moment of inertia \( I \) makes small oscillations about the direction of a uniform field \( B \). Its period is
questions.explanation:
For small \( \theta \), the restoring torque is \( -mB\theta \), so \( I\dfrac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}=-mB\theta \).

This is SHM with \( \omega^2=\dfrac{mB}{I} \), giving \( T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mB}} \).
questions.hint: Inertia goes on top; the restoring strength goes underneath.
distractor_logic: Substitutes the simple pendulum formula; gravity and length play no role in this magnetic oscillation.
Inverts the ratio; inertia should increase the period, not decrease it.
Replaces the magnetic restoring term \( mB \) with a gravitational one.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: The net force on a bar magnet placed in a uniform magnetic field is
options: Largest when the magnet is perpendicular to the field
Equal to the force on the N pole alone
questions.explanation:
In a uniform field, the forces on the two poles are equal in size and opposite in direction.

They cancel, leaving only a couple (a torque), so the net force is zero.
questions.hint: In a uniform field, compare the forces on the two poles.
distractor_logic: Borrows the torque expression; the equal and opposite pole forces cancel.
Describes the torque, not the force.
Ignores the equal and opposite force on the S pole.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: The oscillation of a magnet about its equilibrium direction in a uniform field is simple harmonic only when
options: The magnet starts from the anti-aligned position
The angular displacement is small, so that \( \sin\theta\approx\theta \)
questions.explanation:
The restoring torque is \( mB\sin\theta \). Only for small \( \theta \) does \( \sin\theta\approx\theta \), making the torque proportional to displacement.

That proportionality makes the motion simple harmonic, exactly as for a pendulum at small angles.
questions.hint: SHM needs restoring torque proportional to the angle.
distractor_logic: Anti-alignment is unstable; the magnet swings away rather than oscillating about it.
The standard result assumes a uniform field.
At large amplitudes \( \sin\theta\approx\theta \) fails, so the motion is not SHM.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: Magnetic declination at a place is
options: The angle between the geographic meridian and the magnetic meridian
The angle Earth's total field makes with the horizontal
The angle between Earth's magnetic axis and its rotation axis
The angle between the horizontal and vertical components of Earth's field
questions.explanation:
Declination is measured in the horizontal plane: it tells how far the compass direction (magnetic meridian) deviates from true (geographic) north.

The angle with the horizontal is the dip, a separate element.
questions.hint: Declination tells a navigator how far a compass points away from true north.
distractor_logic: That is the dip, a different element measured in the vertical plane.
That is the global tilt of the magnetic axis, not the local deviation of a compass.
Those components are always perpendicular, so this angle is always \( 90^\circ \).

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: The angle of dip at a place is
options: The angle between the magnetic and geographic meridians
The angle Earth's total magnetic field makes with the horizontal
The angle Earth's total field makes with the vertical
The geographic latitude of the place
questions.explanation:
Dip is measured in the vertical plane of the magnetic meridian, from the horizontal to the direction of \( \vec B \).

It is \( 0^\circ \) at the magnetic equator and \( 90^\circ \) at the magnetic poles.
questions.hint: Dip describes how steeply the field plunges into the ground.
distractor_logic: That is the declination.
That is the complement of the dip.
Dip varies with magnetic latitude but is not equal to geographic latitude.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: The angle of dip at Earth's magnetic equator is
questions.explanation:
At the magnetic equator, Earth's field is horizontal, so \( B_V=0 \).

Hence the dip is \( 0^\circ \).
questions.hint: At the equator, which way does Earth's field point?
distractor_logic: That is the dip at the magnetic poles.
That is where the horizontal and vertical components are equal.
Dip is measured from the horizontal and never exceeds \( 90^\circ \) in magnitude.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: If \( B \) is Earth's total field and \( \delta \) is the dip, the horizontal component is
questions.explanation:
Dip is measured from the horizontal, so the horizontal component is adjacent to \( \delta \).

\( B_H=B\cos\delta \) and \( B_V=B\sin\delta \).
questions.hint: The side adjacent to the angle uses cosine.
distractor_logic: That is the vertical component.
No component is found by multiplying by a tangent.
Divides instead of multiplying; a component cannot exceed the total field.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: The dip \( \delta \) is related to the horizontal and vertical components by
questions.explanation:
\( B_V=B\sin\delta \) and \( B_H=B\cos\delta \).

Dividing: \( \tan\delta=\dfrac{B_V}{B_H} \).
questions.hint: Divide the vertical component by the horizontal one.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; that gives the tangent of the angle with the vertical.
Uses the wrong trigonometric ratio; opposite over adjacent is a tangent.
Uses the wrong trigonometric ratio and the wrong pairing of sides.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: At Earth's magnetic north pole, the horizontal component of Earth's field is
questions.explanation:
At a magnetic pole, the dip is \( 90^\circ \): the field is vertical.

\( B_H=B\cos90^\circ=0 \), which is why an ordinary compass has no preferred direction there.
questions.hint: At a magnetic pole, which way does the field point?
distractor_logic: That describes the vertical component at the poles.
The horizontal component is greatest at the magnetic equator.
That happens only where the dip is \( 45^\circ \).

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: The N end of a compass needle points roughly toward geographic north. The pole of Earth's internal 'bar magnet' located near the geographic north is therefore
options: Not a pole at all, since Earth's field has no poles
questions.explanation:
Unlike poles attract, so the N end of the needle is pulled toward a magnetic S pole.

Hence the pole of Earth's equivalent magnet near geographic north is a magnetic S pole.
questions.hint: Which poles attract each other?
distractor_logic: Unlike poles attract, so the needle's N end must be drawn toward a magnetic S pole.
Earth's field is well described as that of a dipole with two poles.
Isolated magnetic monopoles do not exist; Earth behaves as a dipole.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: According to the currently accepted explanation, Earth's magnetic field arises mainly from
options: A giant permanent magnet of solid iron at the centre
Static electric charges on Earth's surface
Electric currents produced by the motion of molten metallic fluid in Earth's outer core
questions.explanation:
Convective motion of molten metal (mainly iron and nickel) in the outer core forms electric currents.

These currents maintain the field, a process called the dynamo effect.
questions.hint: Moving charges make magnetic fields.
distractor_logic: The core is far hotter than iron's Curie temperature, so permanent magnetization cannot survive.
Static charges produce electric fields, not magnetic ones.
The Moon's field is negligible and could not produce Earth's field.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: The magnetization \( M \) of a material is defined as its
options: Net magnetic moment per unit volume
Net magnetic moment per unit mass
Total magnetic moment of the whole sample
questions.explanation:
\( M=\dfrac{m_{net}}{V} \).

It measures how strongly the material is magnetized, independent of the sample's size.
questions.hint: Think of it as a density of magnetic moment.
distractor_logic: Uses mass instead of volume.
That is \( B \), which also includes the contribution from \( H \).
Omits the division by volume.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: Magnetization \( M \) and magnetic intensity \( H \) share the same SI unit, which is
questions.explanation:
\( M \) is moment per volume: \( \dfrac{\text{A m}^2}{\text{m}^3} \), which is A/m.

\( H \) inside a solenoid is \( nI \): turns per metre times amperes, also A/m.
questions.hint: Divide the unit of magnetic moment by a volume.
distractor_logic: That is the unit of \( B \).
That is the unit of magnetic moment.
That describes susceptibility, the ratio of the two.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: Inside a magnetized material, the magnetic field \( B \) is related to \( H \) and \( M \) by
questions.explanation:
\( H \) accounts for the external (free) currents and \( M \) for the material's own atomic moments.

Both contribute: \( B=\mu_0(H+M) \).
questions.hint: The material adds its own contribution to the field.
distractor_logic: Ignores the material's own magnetization, treating it as vacuum.
Adds \( H \) and \( M \) without the factor \( \mu_0 \).
Subtracts the magnetization; in a magnetized material \( M \) adds to \( H \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: Magnetic susceptibility \( \chi \) is defined as
questions.explanation:
Susceptibility measures how much magnetization a given magnetizing intensity produces.

\( \chi=\dfrac{M}{H} \), a pure number.
questions.hint: Response divided by cause.
distractor_logic: Inverts the defining ratio.
That is the permeability \( \mu \), not the susceptibility.
Divides by the wrong field; susceptibility compares \( M \) with the magnetizing intensity \( H \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: The SI unit of magnetic susceptibility \( \chi \) is
questions.explanation:
\( \chi=\dfrac{M}{H} \) and both have unit A/m.

The units cancel, so \( \chi \) is dimensionless.
questions.hint: Divide two quantities with the same unit.
distractor_logic: That is the unit of \( M \) and \( H \) individually; their ratio has no unit.
That is the unit of permeability.
That is the unit of magnetic moment.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: Relative permeability \( \mu_r \) and susceptibility \( \chi \) are related by
questions.explanation:
\( B=\mu_0(H+M)=\mu_0(1+\chi)H \).

Comparing with \( B=\mu_0\mu_rH \) gives \( \mu_r=1+\chi \).
questions.hint: Vacuum has \( \chi=0 \); what must its \( \mu_r \) be?
distractor_logic: Drops the \( +1 \), treating the two quantities as interchangeable.
Subtracts 1 instead of adding it.
Gets the sign of \( \chi \) wrong.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: The permeability \( \mu \) of a material is given by
questions.explanation:
Relative permeability is defined as \( \mu_r=\dfrac{\mu}{\mu_0} \).

So \( \mu=\mu_0\mu_r \), and \( B=\mu H \).
questions.hint: 'Relative' means compared with vacuum.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \chi \) where \( \mu_r=1+\chi \) belongs.
Divides by \( \mu_0 \) instead of multiplying.
Adds a dimensionless number to a dimensional constant.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: The magnetic intensity \( H \) inside a long solenoid with \( n \) turns per unit length carrying current \( I \) is
questions.explanation:
\( H \) depends only on the free current: \( H=nI \), in A/m.

It does not change when a core is inserted; \( B \) does.
questions.hint: \( H \) has unit A/m: turns per metre times current.
distractor_logic: That is the field \( B \) in an empty solenoid, not \( H \).
That is \( B \) with a core inserted.
Divides instead of multiplying.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: A diamagnetic substance placed in a non-uniform magnetic field
options: Is weakly repelled, moving toward weaker-field regions
Is weakly attracted toward stronger-field regions
questions.explanation:
Diamagnets acquire a small magnetization opposite to the applied field (negative \( \chi \)).

So they are pushed from stronger toward weaker field regions.
questions.hint: Negative susceptibility means opposition to the field.
distractor_logic: That describes a paramagnetic substance.
That describes a ferromagnetic substance.
Diamagnets do experience a weak repulsive force.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: Paramagnetic substances have
options: Small negative \( \chi \), and are weakly repelled
Small positive \( \chi \), and are weakly attracted by a magnet
Large positive \( \chi \), and are strongly attracted
Small positive \( \chi \), and are weakly repelled
questions.explanation:
Paramagnetic atoms carry permanent moments that partly line up with the field.

This gives a small positive \( \chi \) and weak attraction.
questions.hint: 'Para' means alongside the field.
distractor_logic: That describes diamagnetic substances.
That describes ferromagnetic substances.
A positive \( \chi \) means magnetization along the field, which gives attraction, not repulsion.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: Which of these is a diamagnetic substance?
questions.explanation:
Bismuth, copper and water are standard diamagnetic examples.

Aluminium and sodium are paramagnetic; iron is ferromagnetic.
questions.hint: Look for the one repelled by a strong magnet.
distractor_logic: Aluminium is paramagnetic.
Iron is ferromagnetic.
Sodium is paramagnetic.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: Which of these is a ferromagnetic substance?
questions.explanation:
Iron, cobalt and nickel are the standard ferromagnetic examples.

They are strongly attracted by magnets and can be permanently magnetized.
questions.hint: Iron, cobalt and nickel form the familiar trio.
distractor_logic: Copper is diamagnetic.
Oxygen is paramagnetic.
Aluminium is paramagnetic.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: Curie's law for a paramagnetic substance states that its susceptibility is
questions.explanation:
Thermal agitation opposes the alignment of atomic moments.

So paramagnetic susceptibility falls as temperature rises: \( \chi=\dfrac{C}{T} \), with \( T \) in kelvin.
questions.hint: Heat scrambles alignment.
distractor_logic: Makes \( \chi \) increase with temperature; heating actually disturbs alignment.
Uses an inverse-square dependence on temperature.
That describes diamagnets, whose \( \chi \) is essentially temperature-independent.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: Above its Curie temperature, a ferromagnetic substance behaves as
questions.explanation:
Above \( T_C \), thermal agitation breaks up the ordered domains.

The atomic moments remain but align only weakly with an applied field: paramagnetic behaviour.
questions.hint: Heat destroys long-range order but not the atomic moments.
distractor_logic: Heating destroys the domain ordering; it does not strengthen it.
Its atomic moments still exist, so it becomes paramagnetic, not diamagnetic.
Above \( T_C \) all spontaneous magnetization is lost.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: On a B-H hysteresis loop, retentivity is
options: The reverse \( H \) needed to reduce \( B \) to zero
The maximum \( B \) reached at saturation
The value of \( B \) remaining when \( H \) is reduced to zero
The area enclosed by the loop
questions.explanation:
After magnetizing to saturation, reducing \( H \) to zero leaves a residual field.

That residual \( B \), read on the \( B \)-axis, is the retentivity.
questions.hint: Retain: what is left behind when the magnetizing intensity is removed?
distractor_logic: That is coercivity.
Saturation lies at the tip of the loop, not where \( H=0 \).
The loop area measures energy loss per cycle.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: On a B-H hysteresis loop, coercivity is
options: The \( B \) left over when \( H \) returns to zero
The energy dissipated in one cycle
The value of \( H \) at saturation
The magnitude of reverse \( H \) needed to bring \( B \) to zero
questions.explanation:
Coercivity is read on the \( H \)-axis.

It is the reverse magnetizing intensity required to wipe out the residual magnetization.
questions.hint: Coerce: how hard must you push backward to erase the magnetism?
distractor_logic: That is retentivity.
That is represented by the loop area.
Saturation is at the tip of the loop, not on the \( H \)-axis crossing.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: A short bar magnet has moment \( 0.5\ \text{A m}^2 \). Taking \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}=10^{-7} \) T m/A, find the field at 0.1 m on its axis.
questions.hint: Cube the distance: \( (0.1)^3=10^{-3} \).
distractor_logic: Uses the equatorial formula, which lacks the factor 2.
Divides by \( r^2 \) instead of \( r^3 \).

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: A short bar magnet has moment \( 0.8\ \text{A m}^2 \). Taking \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}=10^{-7} \) T m/A, find the field at 0.2 m on its equatorial line.
questions.hint: \( (0.2)^3=0.008 \), and there is no factor 2 on the equatorial line.
distractor_logic: Uses the axial formula with its factor 2.
Divides by \( r^2 \) instead of \( r^3 \).
Divides by \( r \) alone, as for a straight wire.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: The field at a point on the axis of a short bar magnet is \( B_0 \). What is the field magnitude at a point on its equatorial line at the same distance?
questions.explanation:
At equal distances, \( B_{axial}:B_{eq}=2:1 \).

So \( B_{eq}=\dfrac{B_0}{2} \).
questions.hint: Which line carries the extra factor 2?
distractor_logic: Swaps the 2:1 ratio, making the equatorial field the larger one.
Assumes equal distances give equal fields, ignoring the factor 2.
Cubes the factor 2 as though the distance had changed.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: The distance of an axial point from a short bar magnet is doubled. The field there becomes
questions.explanation:
\( B\propto\dfrac{1}{r^3} \).

Doubling \( r \) divides \( B \) by \( 2^3=8 \).
questions.hint: Dipole fields fall as the cube of distance.
distractor_logic: Uses an inverse-square law.
Uses a simple inverse proportion to distance.
Uses a \( 1/r^4 \) fall-off.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: A bar magnet of moment \( m \) is cut into two equal halves perpendicular to its length. Each half is
options: A complete magnet with its own N and S poles, of moment \( \dfrac{m}{2} \)
An isolated N pole or an isolated S pole
A complete magnet of moment \( m \)
questions.explanation:
Cutting never isolates a pole: fresh N and S poles appear at the cut, because magnetic monopoles do not exist.

Pole strength stays the same while the magnetic length halves, so each piece has moment \( \dfrac{m}{2} \).
questions.hint: \( m \) equals pole strength times magnetic length.
distractor_logic: Assumes cutting separates the poles; isolated monopoles never exist, and new poles appear at the cut.
Keeps the full moment even though the pole separation has been halved.
Halves both pole strength and length; a cut perpendicular to the axis leaves pole strength unchanged.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: A bar magnet has pole strength \( 5\ \text{A m} \) and magnetic length 0.1 m. Its magnetic moment is
questions.explanation:
\( m=q_m\times(2l)=5\times0.1 \)

\( =0.5\ \text{A m}^2 \)
questions.hint: Multiply pole strength by the full distance between the poles.
distractor_logic: Divides pole strength by length instead of multiplying.
Uses half the magnetic length.
Ignores the length and reports the pole strength as the moment.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: For a short bar magnet, what is the ratio of the field at distance \( r \) on its axis to the field at distance \( 2r \) on its equatorial line?
questions.explanation:
\( B_{axial}(r)=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3} \) and \( B_{eq}(2r)=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{8r^3} \).

Ratio \( =\dfrac{2}{1/8}=16 \), i.e. \( 16:1 \).
questions.hint: Combine the factor 2 with the \( 2^3 \) from the distance.
distractor_logic: Ignores the different distances and keeps only the axial factor 2.
Keeps the \( 2^3 \) distance factor but drops the axial factor 2.
Uses an inverse-square law and drops the axial factor 2.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: Inside a bar magnet, the magnetic field \( \vec B \) points
options: Opposite to \( \vec m \), as it does between the charges of an electric dipole
Nowhere, because the field exists only outside the magnet
Along \( \vec m \), from the S pole to the N pole
questions.explanation:
Field lines leave N, go around outside, enter S, and return inside from S to N.

Since \( \vec m \) points from S to N, the interior field is along \( \vec m \), unlike an electric dipole, whose field between the charges points opposite to \( \vec p \).
questions.hint: Follow one closed loop back through the magnet.
distractor_logic: Carries over the electric dipole, whose field between the charges opposes \( \vec p \); magnetic lines continue from S to N inside.
Magnetic lines are closed loops and must pass through the magnet.
The interior lines run along the axis, not across it.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet of moment \( 2\ \text{A m}^2 \) makes \( 30^\circ \) with a uniform field of 0.5 T. The magnitude of the torque on it is
questions.explanation:
\( \tau=mB\sin\theta=2\times0.5\times\sin30^\circ \)

\( =1\times\dfrac12=0.5 \) N m
questions.hint: Torque uses the sine of the angle.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \cos30^\circ \) instead of \( \sin30^\circ \).
Ignores \( \sin\theta \), giving the maximum torque \( mB \).

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet of moment \( 4\ \text{A m}^2 \) makes \( 60^\circ \) with a uniform field of 0.5 T. Its potential energy is
questions.explanation:
\( U=-mB\cos\theta=-4\times0.5\times\cos60^\circ \)

\( =-2\times\dfrac12=-1 \) J
questions.hint: Energy uses cosine, with a minus sign.
distractor_logic: Drops the minus sign in \( U=-mB\cos\theta \).
Uses \( \sin60^\circ \) instead of \( \cos60^\circ \).
Reports the torque magnitude \( mB\sin\theta \) as the energy.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: How much work is needed to turn a magnet of moment \( 1.5\ \text{A m}^2 \) from alignment with a 0.2 T field to exact anti-alignment?
questions.hint: Work equals final energy minus initial energy.
distractor_logic: Computes only \( mB \), the work to turn from \( 0^\circ \) to \( 90^\circ \).
Sees equal magnitudes of \( U \) at the two ends and ignores the sign change from \( -mB \) to \( +mB \).

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet with \( I=5\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^2 \) and \( m=0.5\ \text{A m}^2 \) makes small oscillations in a uniform 0.04 T field. Its period is
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{I}{mB}=\dfrac{5\times10^{-3}}{0.5\times0.04}=\dfrac{5\times10^{-3}}{2\times10^{-2}}=0.25\ \text{s}^2 \).

\( T=2\pi\sqrt{0.25}=2\pi\times0.5=\pi \) s
questions.hint: Compute \( \dfrac{I}{mB} \) first, then take the square root.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \dfrac{mB}{I} \) under the square root, inverting the ratio.
Forgets to take the square root of \( \dfrac{I}{mB} \).
Reports the frequency \( 1/T \) instead of the period.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet oscillates in a uniform field with period \( T \). If the field is made 4 times stronger (small oscillations), the new period is
questions.explanation:
\( T\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt B} \).

With \( 4B \), \( T'=\dfrac{T}{\sqrt4}=\dfrac{T}{2} \).
questions.hint: Field sits under a square root in the denominator.
distractor_logic: Assumes a stronger field slows the oscillation; stronger restoring torque speeds it up.
Forgets the square root in the period formula.
Assumes the period depends only on the magnet, as a pendulum's depends only on length and gravity.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: At what angle between \( \vec m \) and \( \vec B \) is the torque on a magnet half of its maximum value (taking the angle below \( 90^\circ \))?
questions.explanation:
\( mB\sin\theta=\dfrac12mB\Rightarrow\sin\theta=\dfrac12 \).

So \( \theta=30^\circ \).
questions.hint: Set \( \sin\theta \) equal to one half.
distractor_logic: Solves \( \cos\theta=\dfrac12 \) instead of \( \sin\theta=\dfrac12 \).

questions.question: A magnet in a 0.02 T field experiences a torque of 0.03 N m when it makes \( 30^\circ \) with the field. Its magnetic moment is

\( m=\dfrac{\tau}{B\sin\theta}=\dfrac{0.03}{0.02\times0.5} \)

\( =\dfrac{0.03}{0.01}=3\ \text{A m}^2 \)

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: At a place where the dip is \( 45^\circ \), the horizontal component is \( 3\times10^{-5} \) T. The vertical component is
questions.explanation:
\( B_V=B_H\tan\delta=3\times10^{-5}\times\tan45^\circ \)

\( =3\times10^{-5}\times1=3\times10^{-5} \) T

distractor_logic: That is the total field, not the vertical component.
Multiplies \( B_H \) by \( \sin45^\circ \) instead of \( \tan45^\circ \).

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components

\( \tan\delta=\dfrac{B_V}{B_H}=1 \).

So \( \delta=45^\circ \).

distractor_logic: Assumes equal components cancel; they are perpendicular and cannot cancel.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components

questions.explanation:
The components are perpendicular, so \( B=\sqrt{B_H^2+B_V^2} \).

\( B=\sqrt{9+16}\times10^{-5}=5\times10^{-5} \) T

distractor_logic: Adds the perpendicular components as scalars.
Subtracts the components.

questions.explanation:
\( B_V=B\sin\delta\Rightarrow B=\dfrac{B_V}{\sin30^\circ} \).

\( B=\dfrac{2\times10^{-5}}{1/2}=4\times10^{-5} \) T

questions.question: At a place where the dip is \( 60^\circ \), the ratio \( \dfrac{B_V}{B_H} \) is

\( \dfrac{B_V}{B_H}=\tan\delta=\tan60^\circ \).

\( =\sqrt3 \)
questions.hint: The ratio of components is the tangent of the dip.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio, giving \( \dfrac{B_H}{B_V} \).

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: At a place, a freely pivoted horizontal compass needle settles pointing \( 15^\circ \) west of geographic north. The declination at that place is
options: Zero, since the compass defines north
questions.explanation:
Declination is the angle between the magnetic meridian (the needle's direction) and the geographic meridian.

The needle is \( 15^\circ \) west of true north, so the declination is \( 15^\circ \) west.
questions.hint: Declination is the angle between the needle and true north.

questions.explanation:

questions.question: A material has relative permeability 500. Its magnetic susceptibility is

\( \chi=500-1=499 \), dimensionless.

\( M=\chi H=2\times10^{-3}\times500 \)

\( =1 \) A/m
questions.hint: \( M=\chi H \).
distractor_logic: Divides \( H \) by \( \chi \) instead of multiplying.
Divides \( \chi \) by \( H \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility

questions.hint: Add \( H \) and \( M \) first, then multiply by \( \mu_0 \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( B=\mu_0H \), ignoring the material's magnetization.
Adds \( H \) and \( M \) without the factor \( \mu_0 \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: A diamagnetic material has \( \chi=-10^{-5} \). Its relative permeability is
questions.explanation:
\( \mu_r=1+\chi=1+(-10^{-5}) \).

\( \mu_r=0.99999 \), slightly less than 1, as expected for a diamagnet.
questions.hint: A negative \( \chi \) makes \( \mu_r \) slightly less than 1.
distractor_logic: Ignores the negative sign of the diamagnetic susceptibility.
Reports \( \chi \) as \( \mu_r \), dropping the 1.
Drops both the 1 and the negative sign.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: In a material, \( B=4\pi\times10^{-3} \) T when \( H=100 \) A/m. Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, the susceptibility is
questions.explanation:
\( \mu=\dfrac{B}{H}=4\pi\times10^{-5} \) T m/A, so \( \mu_r=\dfrac{\mu}{\mu_0}=100 \).

\( \chi=\mu_r-1=99 \), dimensionless.
questions.hint: Find \( \mu_r \) first, then subtract 1.
distractor_logic: Reports \( \mu_r \) instead of \( \chi \).
Adds 1 to \( \mu_r \) instead of subtracting.
Reports the permeability \( \dfrac{B}{H} \) in T m/A.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: In a material, \( H=500 \) A/m and \( B=2\pi\times10^{-3} \) T. Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, the magnetization is
options: Zero, since \( B \) is set by \( H \) alone
questions.hint: Solve \( B=\mu_0(H+M) \) for \( M \).
distractor_logic: Takes \( \dfrac{B}{\mu_0} \) as \( M \), forgetting to subtract \( H \).
Adds \( H \) instead of subtracting it.
Uses \( B=\mu_0H \), treating the material as vacuum.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: A soft-iron core is slid into a long solenoid while the current is kept constant. As a result,
options: Both \( B \) and \( H \) increase by the factor \( \mu_r \)
\( H \) increases, but \( B \) stays at \( \mu_0nI \)
\( B \) increases greatly, but \( H \) stays equal to \( nI \)
questions.explanation:
\( H=nI \) is fixed by the current and the winding.

The iron becomes strongly magnetized, so \( B=\mu_0(H+M) \) rises sharply.
questions.hint: Which quantity depends only on the current?
distractor_logic: \( H \) depends only on the free current; the core adds magnetization \( M \), not \( H \).
Swaps the roles of \( B \) and \( H \).
Ignores the core's magnetization, treating iron as vacuum.

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: A material has \( \mu_r=1.0002 \). In a magnetic intensity of 5000 A/m, its magnetization is
questions.hint: Convert \( \mu_r \) to \( \chi \) first.
distractor_logic: Multiplies \( H \) by \( \mu_r \) instead of by \( \chi \).
Divides \( H \) by \( \chi \).
Divides \( \chi \) by \( H \).

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: A paramagnetic salt has susceptibility \( \chi_0 \) at 300 K. At 600 K (same applied field), its susceptibility is
questions.explanation:
Curie's law: \( \chi\propto\dfrac1T \).

Doubling \( T \) from 300 K to 600 K halves \( \chi \): \( \dfrac{\chi_0}{2} \).
questions.hint: Susceptibility is inversely proportional to absolute temperature.
distractor_logic: Makes susceptibility increase with temperature, reversing Curie's law.
Treats the salt as temperature-independent, as a diamagnet would be.
Uses an inverse-square temperature dependence.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: A paramagnet has susceptibility \( \chi_0 \) at \( 27^\circ\text{C} \). Its susceptibility at \( 327^\circ\text{C} \) is
questions.explanation:
Convert to kelvin: \( 27^\circ\text{C}=300 \) K and \( 327^\circ\text{C}=600 \) K.

\( \dfrac{\chi_2}{\chi_1}=\dfrac{300}{600} \), so \( \chi_2=\dfrac{\chi_0}{2} \).
questions.hint: Curie's law needs absolute temperature.
distractor_logic: Uses Celsius temperatures directly in the ratio instead of kelvin.
Makes susceptibility increase with temperature.
Uses Celsius values and also inverts the ratio.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: A material suitable for making a permanent magnet should have
questions.explanation:
A permanent magnet must keep a strong residual field: high retentivity.

It must also resist demagnetization: high coercivity, giving a wide (hard) hysteresis loop.
questions.hint: Strong and hard to erase.
distractor_logic: Low coercivity lets stray fields or knocks demagnetize it easily.
Low retentivity leaves too weak a residual field.
That describes a soft material, the opposite of what a permanent magnet needs.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: The core of an electromagnet should be made of a material with
options: High coercivity and a wide hysteresis loop
Negative susceptibility, as in a diamagnet
Small positive susceptibility, as in a paramagnet
Low coercivity and a thin hysteresis loop, so it magnetizes strongly but loses its magnetization readily when the current stops
questions.explanation:
An electromagnet must switch on and off with the current.

A soft ferromagnet (such as soft iron), with high permeability and low coercivity, magnetizes strongly yet demagnetizes easily and wastes little energy per cycle.
questions.hint: It must be easy to switch off.
distractor_logic: That suits a permanent magnet; the core would stay magnetized after switch-off.
A diamagnetic core would weaken the field.
Paramagnetic \( \chi \) is tiny; the core must be ferromagnetic to give a large \( \mu_r \).

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: The area enclosed by a material's B-H hysteresis loop represents
options: The energy dissipated as heat per unit volume in each magnetization cycle
The permanent magnetic moment stored in the sample
questions.explanation:
Taking a material around its loop requires work that is not recovered.

That lost energy, proportional to the loop area, appears as heat.
questions.hint: A fat loop means a hot core.
distractor_logic: Retentivity is a single value of \( B \) at \( H=0 \).
Coercivity is a single value of \( H \) at \( B=0 \).
The loop area is an energy loss, not a stored moment.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: A superconductor below its critical temperature is best described as
options: A perfect diamagnet with \( \chi=-1 \), expelling magnetic field lines
A material with very large positive \( \chi \), like a ferromagnet
questions.explanation:
With \( \chi=-1 \), \( M=-H \) and \( B=\mu_0(H+M)=0 \) inside.

The field is completely expelled; this is the Meissner effect.
questions.hint: Complete opposition to the field.
distractor_logic: Gets the sign wrong; superconductors oppose the field completely.
Vacuum lets field lines through; a superconductor expels them.
Ferromagnets concentrate field lines, the opposite of expulsion.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: How does the susceptibility of a diamagnetic substance such as bismuth vary with temperature?
options: It becomes positive at high temperature
It stays small and negative, essentially independent of temperature
It increases in proportion to \( T \)
questions.explanation:
Diamagnetism arises from induced changes in electron orbits, which thermal motion barely affects.

So \( \chi \) stays small, negative, and essentially independent of temperature.
questions.hint: There are no permanent moments for heat to scramble.
distractor_logic: Curie's law applies to paramagnets, not diamagnets.
Diamagnetic \( \chi \) remains negative.
No standard material has susceptibility proportional to temperature.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: A narrow arm of a U-tube containing water (a diamagnetic liquid) is placed between the poles of a strong electromagnet. The water level in that arm
questions.explanation:
Water is diamagnetic, so it is pushed out of the strong-field region.

The level between the poles drops slightly.
questions.hint: Diamagnets move away from strong fields.
distractor_logic: That is what a paramagnetic liquid does.
That would suggest strong ferromagnetic attraction.
Water is weakly repelled, so a small change does occur.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: Two identical short magnets, each of moment \( 1\ \text{A m}^2 \), both point along \( +x \). Magnet P sits at the origin, and point X is at \( (0.1\ \text{m},\,0) \) on P's axis. Magnet Q sits at \( (0.1\ \text{m},\,-0.1\ \text{m}) \), so X lies on Q's equatorial line. Taking \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}=10^{-7} \) T m/A, the net field at X is
questions.explanation:
From P (axial): \( 10^{-7}\times\dfrac{2\times1}{10^{-3}}=2\times10^{-4} \) T along \( +x \).

From Q (equatorial): \( 10^{-7}\times\dfrac{1}{10^{-3}}=10^{-4} \) T, opposite to \( \vec m \), i.e. along \( -x \).

Net: \( 2\times10^{-4}-10^{-4}=10^{-4} \) T along \( +x \).
questions.hint: The equatorial field points opposite to the magnet's moment.
distractor_logic: Adds the magnitudes, missing that the equatorial field points opposite to \( \vec m \).
Treats the two fields as perpendicular; both lie along the x-axis.
Assumes the axial and equatorial fields are equal and cancel, forgetting the 2:1 ratio.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: At distance \( r_1 \) on the axis of a short magnet, the field equals the field at distance \( r_2 \) on its equatorial line. The ratio \( \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} \) is
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{2m}{r_1^3}=\dfrac{m}{r_2^3}\Rightarrow r_1^3=2r_2^3 \).

So \( \dfrac{r_1}{r_2}=2^{1/3} \); the axial point lies farther out.
questions.hint: The axial point must be farther away to weaken its stronger field.
distractor_logic: Equates \( 2/r_1 \) with \( 1/r_2 \), forgetting the cube.
Uses an inverse-square law.
Inverts the ratio; the axial point must be farther away to weaken its larger field.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: A closed surface encloses only the N-pole end of a bar magnet; the surface slices through the body of the magnet. The net magnetic flux through this surface is
options: Positive, equal to the flux of the lines leaving the N pole
Negative, because the interior field points into the enclosed region
questions.explanation:
Inside the magnet, lines run from S to N, so they enter the enclosed region through the slice.

The same lines leave through the outer part of the surface. Inflow equals outflow, so the net flux is zero; Gauss's law holds for every closed surface.
questions.hint: Follow a single closed loop: how many times does it cross the surface inward and outward?
distractor_logic: Counts only the outward lines outside the magnet and misses the equal flux entering through the slice inside the magnet.
Treats the enclosed pole as a magnetic charge, copying the electric Gauss's law.
Counts only the lines entering through the slice and ignores those leaving outside.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: The field at 20 cm on the axis of a short bar magnet is \( B \). The field at 10 cm on its equatorial line is
questions.hint: Halving the distance multiplies by 8; moving to the equatorial line divides by 2.
distractor_logic: Applies only the 2:1 axial-to-equatorial ratio and ignores the change in distance.
Applies the \( 2^3 \) distance factor but forgets the axial factor 2.
Uses an inverse-square law for the distance change.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: A short solenoid of 100 turns and cross-sectional area \( 2\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2 \) carries 0.5 A and behaves like a bar magnet. Taking \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}=10^{-7} \) T m/A, the field at 0.1 m on its axis is
questions.hint: First find the solenoid's equivalent moment \( NIA \).
distractor_logic: Uses the equatorial formula, which lacks the factor 2.
Divides by \( r^2 \) instead of \( r^3 \).
Forgets the number of turns when finding the moment.

questions.topic: The Bar Magnet as a Magnetic Dipole: Field Lines, Axial and Equatorial Fields, and Gauss's Law for Magnetism
questions.question: Two identical short magnets, each of moment \( m \), are placed at the same point at right angles to each other. At distance \( r \) along the direction of their resultant moment, the field is
questions.explanation:
Moments add as vectors: \( m_{net}=\sqrt{m^2+m^2}=\sqrt2\,m \).

The point lies on the axis of this resultant dipole, so \( B=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2\sqrt2\,m}{r^3} \).
questions.hint: Magnetic moments are vectors.
distractor_logic: Adds the moments as scalars to get \( 2m \).
Uses the equatorial formula although the point lies on the resultant axis.
Uses the electric constant instead of \( \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \).

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet with \( I=10^{-4}\ \text{kg m}^2 \) and \( m=1\ \text{A m}^2 \) makes small oscillations in a uniform field with period \( 0.2\pi \) s. The field strength is
questions.hint: Square both sides of the period formula before solving for \( B \).
distractor_logic: Sets \( \dfrac{T}{2\pi} \) equal to \( \dfrac{I}{mB} \), forgetting to square it.
Uses the inverted formula \( T=2\pi\sqrt{mB/I} \).
Solves for \( B \) upside down, putting \( I \) in the denominator.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet of moment \( 2\ \text{A m}^2 \) in a 0.1 T field is turned from \( 60^\circ \) to \( 180^\circ \) with the field. The work needed is
questions.hint: Find \( U \) at each angle, then subtract.
distractor_logic: Takes \( U_{60} \) as \( +0.1 \) J, dropping its minus sign.
Uses \( 2mB \), the work from \( 0^\circ \), not from \( 60^\circ \).
Subtracts in the wrong order; energy must be supplied.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet with \( m=0.5\ \text{A m}^2 \) and \( I=10^{-3}\ \text{kg m}^2 \) is released from rest at \( 90^\circ \) to a uniform 0.1 T field. Ignoring friction, its angular speed as it passes the field direction is
questions.explanation:
Energy released: \( U_{90}-U_{0}=0-(-mB)=mB=0.05 \) J.

\( \dfrac12I\omega^2=0.05\Rightarrow\omega^2=\dfrac{0.1}{10^{-3}}=100 \), so \( \omega=10 \) rad/s.
questions.hint: Use energy conservation; the drop in \( U \) becomes rotational kinetic energy.
distractor_logic: Drops the factor \( \dfrac12 \) in the rotational kinetic energy.
Forgets to take the square root of \( \omega^2 \).
Uses an energy drop of \( 2mB \), which corresponds to release from \( 180^\circ \), not \( 90^\circ \).

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: Two magnets of moments \( 5\ \text{A m}^2 \) and \( 3\ \text{A m}^2 \) are fastened together and oscillate in the same uniform field. With their moments pointing the same way the period is \( T_s \); with moments pointing opposite ways it is \( T_d \). The total moment of inertia is the same in both cases. The ratio \( \dfrac{T_d}{T_s} \) is
questions.explanation:
Same direction: \( m=5+3=8\ \text{A m}^2 \). Opposite: \( m=5-3=2\ \text{A m}^2 \).

\( \dfrac{T_d}{T_s}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8}{2}}=2 \)
questions.hint: \( T\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt m} \) when \( I \) and \( B \) are fixed.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio; the smaller net moment gives the longer period.
Forgets the square root in the period formula.
Inverts the ratio and also drops the square root.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet held exactly anti-aligned with a uniform field is given a very slight twist and released. It
options: Stays at its new angle, since the torque is zero at \( 180^\circ \)
Turns away from \( 180^\circ \) and swings toward the aligned direction, because \( 180^\circ \) is an unstable equilibrium
Returns to \( 180^\circ \), since \( U \) is minimum there
questions.explanation:
At \( 180^\circ \), \( U=+mB \), the maximum possible value.

Any small twist produces a torque that increases the displacement, so the magnet moves toward \( \theta=0^\circ \), where \( U=-mB \) is minimum.
questions.hint: Which way does a ball go when nudged off a hilltop?
distractor_logic: That period applies to oscillation about the stable position, not the unstable one.
Zero torque exactly at \( 180^\circ \) does not mean zero torque once displaced; this is not a neutral equilibrium.
Swaps the extremes; \( U=+mB \) at \( 180^\circ \) is the maximum.

questions.topic: Torque, Potential Energy, and Oscillations of a Bar Magnet in a Uniform Magnetic Field
questions.question: A magnet oscillates with period \( T \) in a uniform field. Its moment is reduced to half (moment of inertia unchanged), and it is placed in a field twice as strong. For small oscillations, the new period is
questions.explanation:
\( T\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{mB}} \).

New product: \( \dfrac m2\times2B=mB \), unchanged, so the period stays \( T \).
questions.hint: Only the product \( mB \) matters.
distractor_logic: Applies only the doubling of the field.
Applies only the halving of the moment.
Uses \( T\propto\dfrac1B \) without the square root and ignores the change in moment.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: At a place, the horizontal component of Earth's field is \( \sqrt3 \) times the vertical component, and \( B_H=3\times10^{-5} \) T. The total field is
questions.explanation:
\( \tan\delta=\dfrac{B_V}{B_H}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow\delta=30^\circ \).

\( B=\dfrac{B_H}{\cos30^\circ}=\dfrac{3\times10^{-5}\times2}{\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3\times10^{-5} \) T
questions.hint: Find the dip first from the ratio of components.
distractor_logic: Divides \( B_H \) by \( \sin30^\circ \), effectively taking the dip as \( 60^\circ \).
Multiplies \( B_H \) by \( \cos30^\circ \) instead of dividing.
Swaps the components, taking \( B_V=\sqrt3\,B_H \) and reporting that.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: Earth's total field has the same magnitude at two places, but the dip is \( 30^\circ \) at P and \( 60^\circ \) at Q. The ratio of horizontal components \( \dfrac{B_{H,P}}{B_{H,Q}} \) is
questions.explanation:
\( B_H=B\cos\delta \), with the same \( B \) at both places.

\( \dfrac{B_{H,P}}{B_{H,Q}}=\dfrac{\cos30^\circ}{\cos60^\circ}=\dfrac{\sqrt3/2}{1/2}=\sqrt3 \)
questions.hint: Same total field: compare the cosines of the dips.
distractor_logic: Uses sines of the dips, which compares the vertical components.
Takes the ratio of the dip angles themselves.
Assumes equal total fields mean equal horizontal components.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: As a traveller moves from Earth's magnetic equator toward a magnetic pole,
options: The dip decreases to \( 0^\circ \), while \( B_H \) increases
The dip increases, and \( B_H \) also increases
The dip increases from \( 0^\circ \) to \( 90^\circ \), while \( B_H \) decreases to zero
Both the dip and \( B_H \) stay constant
questions.explanation:
At the equator the field is horizontal (dip \( 0^\circ \)); at a pole it is vertical (dip \( 90^\circ \)).

As the dip grows, \( B_H=B\cos\delta \) shrinks, reaching zero at the pole.
questions.hint: Picture the field turning from horizontal to vertical.
distractor_logic: Reverses both trends; the field becomes more vertical near the poles.
Assumes a stronger total field means a stronger horizontal part; near a pole the field turns vertical.
Earth's field direction changes markedly with magnetic latitude.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: At a place where the dip is \( 45^\circ \), the vertical component of Earth's field is \( 2\times10^{-5} \) T. The total field is
questions.explanation:
At \( 45^\circ \), \( B_H=B_V=2\times10^{-5} \) T.

\( B=\sqrt{B_H^2+B_V^2}=2\sqrt2\times10^{-5} \) T
questions.hint: At \( 45^\circ \) dip, both components are equal.
distractor_logic: Adds \( B_H \) and \( B_V \) as scalars.
Multiplies \( B_V \) by \( \sin45^\circ \) instead of dividing.
Reports a single component; the total field is larger than either component.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: At a place, the declination is \( 5^\circ \) east (magnetic north lies \( 5^\circ \) east of true north). To travel toward true north, a navigator should steer
options: \( 5^\circ \) west of the direction the compass needle points
\( 5^\circ \) east of the direction the compass needle points
questions.explanation:
The needle points to magnetic north, which is \( 5^\circ \) east of true north.

So true north lies \( 5^\circ \) west of the needle's direction.
questions.hint: Sketch true north and the needle direction.
distractor_logic: Applies the correction in the wrong direction.
Ignores declination; the needle shows magnetic north, not true north.
Uses the complement of the declination.

questions.topic: Elements of Earth's Magnetism: Declination, Dip, and Horizontal/Vertical Components
questions.question: At a place where the dip is \( 30^\circ \) and Earth's total field is \( 10^{-4} \) T, the components are
questions.explanation:
\( B_H=B\cos30^\circ=10^{-4}\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=5\sqrt3\times10^{-5} \) T.

\( B_V=B\sin30^\circ=10^{-4}\times\dfrac12=5\times10^{-5} \) T
questions.hint: A small dip means the field is mostly horizontal.
distractor_logic: Swaps sine and cosine, which corresponds to a \( 60^\circ \) dip.
Splits the field equally, ignoring the dip.
Takes the whole field as horizontal, violating \( B^2=B_H^2+B_V^2 \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: A long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carries 2 A and is filled with a core of \( \mu_r=400 \). The magnetization of the core is
questions.hint: Find \( H \) from the winding, then use \( \chi \), not \( \mu_r \).
distractor_logic: Uses \( \mu_r \) in place of \( \chi \).
Reports \( H \) instead of \( M \).
Takes \( \chi=\mu_r+1 \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: A long solenoid with 1000 turns per metre carries 2 A and is filled with a core of \( \mu_r=400 \). Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, the field \( B \) inside the core is
questions.explanation:
\( B=\mu_0\mu_rnI=4\pi\times10^{-7}\times400\times2000 \).

\( =4\pi\times10^{-7}\times8\times10^{5}=0.32\pi \) T
distractor_logic: Uses \( B=\mu_0nI \), ignoring the core.
Multiplies by \( \chi \) instead of \( \mu_r \), losing the contribution of \( H \).
Omits \( \mu_0 \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: A superconductor is a perfect diamagnet with \( \chi=-1 \). In an applied intensity \( H \), inside it
questions.explanation:
\( M=\chi H=-H \).

\( B=\mu_0(H+M)=\mu_0(H-H)=0 \): the field is completely expelled.
questions.hint: Put \( \chi=-1 \) into \( M=\chi H \), then into \( B=\mu_0(H+M) \).
distractor_logic: Uses a positive susceptibility.
Finds \( M \) correctly but then uses \( B=\mu_0H \), ignoring \( M \).
Zero field does not mean zero magnetization; \( M \) exactly cancels \( H \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: In a material, \( H=4000 \) A/m and \( B=0.8\pi \) T. Taking \( \mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7} \) T m/A, the susceptibility is
questions.hint: Get \( M \) from \( B=\mu_0(H+M) \), then divide by \( H \).
distractor_logic: Reports \( \mu_r \), not \( \chi \).
Reports \( M \) in A/m instead of the ratio \( \dfrac{M}{H} \).
Inverts the ratio, computing \( \dfrac{H}{M} \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: A diamagnetic sample is placed where the magnetic intensity \( \vec H \) points east. Its magnetization \( \vec M \) points
questions.explanation:
\( \vec M=\chi\vec H \) with \( \chi \) negative for a diamagnet.

So \( \vec M \) is antiparallel to \( \vec H \): it points west.
questions.hint: What is the sign of \( \chi \) for a diamagnet?
distractor_logic: That is paramagnetic behaviour; diamagnets have negative \( \chi \).
Diamagnets do magnetize, weakly; \( M \) is small, not zero.
For these simple materials \( \vec M=\chi\vec H \) lies along the line of \( \vec H \).

questions.topic: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity, and Magnetic Susceptibility
questions.question: Starting from \( B=\mu_0(H+M) \), the ratio \( \dfrac{B}{\mu_0H} \) equals
questions.explanation:
\( \dfrac{B}{\mu_0H}=\dfrac{H+M}{H}=1+\dfrac{M}{H} \).

This is \( 1+\chi \), i.e. \( \mu_r \): susceptibility and relative permeability differ by exactly 1.
questions.hint: Divide both terms in the bracket by \( H \).
distractor_logic: Drops the term coming from \( H \) itself.
Inverts the magnetization ratio.
Keeps an extra \( \mu_0 \) after already dividing by it.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: A paramagnetic sample has \( \chi=3\times10^{-4} \) at \( -73^\circ\text{C} \). Its susceptibility at \( 327^\circ\text{C} \) is
questions.explanation:
Convert to kelvin: \( T_1=200 \) K and \( T_2=600 \) K.

\( \dfrac{\chi_2}{\chi_1}=\dfrac{T_1}{T_2}=\dfrac{200}{600}=\dfrac13 \), so \( \chi_2=10^{-4} \).
questions.hint: Convert both temperatures to kelvin first.
distractor_logic: Makes susceptibility increase with temperature.
Ignores the temperature change.

questions.topic: Magnetic Properties of Materials: Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic Substances, and Hysteresis
questions.question: Rods of iron, aluminium and bismuth, and an empty region (vacuum), are placed in the same uniform field. Ranked from densest to sparsest field lines inside, the order is

Iron, then aluminium, then vacuum, then bismuth
Iron, then bismuth, then aluminium, then vacuum
Aluminium, then iron, then vacuum, then bismuth

X for an electromagnet core, Y for a permanent magnet
